Neonates of the red-bellied black snake emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a snout-vent length of 24 cm [Lb = 24 cm], a modest size that nonetheless positions them well for immediate foraging on small frogs and lizards. This initial body dimension is complemented by a birth mass estimated at 5 grams [Wwb = 5 grams], a value derived from closely related elapids of similar ecology, such as the tiger snake. The juvenile period is marked by rapid somatic growth, with individuals investing heavily in axial elongation and muscular development to effectively subdue prey. During this phase, young snakes are particularly vulnerable to avian and mammalian predators, and their cryptic coloration provides essential camouflage among leaf litter and riparian vegetation. The transition from yolk-dependent embryo to active predator is completed within days of hatching, as the residual yolk reserves are fully absorbed and the first exogenous feeding event occurs. This early life stage is critical for establishing the growth trajectory that will ultimately determine adult body size and reproductive potential, underscoring the importance of habitat quality and prey availability in the months following emergence from the nest.

Sexual maturity in the red-bellied black snake is reached at a snout-vent length of 88 cm [Lp = 88 cm] in females and 78 cm [Lp = 78 cm] in males, with females requiring a somewhat larger body size before the onset of reproductive capability. Fully grown adults attain an ultimate snout-vent length of 120 cm [Li = 120 cm] in females and up to 150 cm [Li = up to 150 cm] in males, with the corresponding ultimate wet weight for the largest individuals reaching approximately 1000 grams [Wwi = approximately 1000 grams]. Field and captive longevity records indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 11.6 years [am = approximately 11.6 years] for this species at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C].
